title: The Evolution of a Short Seller | Frederick Shad Rowe | Talks at Google
description:
Frederick "Shad" Rowe is a long-only consumer focused investor with a stellar track record over 3 decades. In this talk, Shad shares stories from his days as a short seller in the 80s, his model of three stages of a company, the philosophy of better-faster-cheaper, and the art of customer focus.

Moderated by Pranesh Srinivasan.
summary: The video argues that successful large companies often share common traits such as global reach, a massive customer base, and the ability to expand their product offerings. It suggests that companies like Southwest Airlines, Starbucks, Costco, and Amazon have achieved success by evolving through specific stages of growth and operational efficiency. Additionally, the speaker highlights the importance of customer service responses, noting that heroic gestures from companies like Constellation Brands can lead to significant investment profits, whereas standard responses from others like McDonald's are less impactful.

claims.claim: The speaker teases that all large companies, including Google, are good because they have a large number of customers and operate globally.
claims.quote: Well, all of them, really. You know, Southwest Airlines now is going to Mexico. They're going in the Caribbean. They're big enough to do it, and no one would sit aside and let Southwest do to them what they did.
claims.speaker: FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE

claims.claim: Southwest Airlines is described as a stage one company that has been successful throughout its career due to being big enough to expand globally.
claims.quote: Southwest Airlines now is going to Mexico. They're going in the Caribbean. They're big enough to do it, and no one would sit aside and let Southwest do to them what they did. I mean, Southwest, I think couldn't happen again, because people are just smarter.
claims.speaker: FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE

claims.claim: Starbucks is cited as a stage two company that successfully expanded by selling tea and food to get more money from the same person.
claims.quote: And stage two is maybe like a Starbucks, where they start selling tea and different food and trying to get more money from the same person.
claims.speaker: FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE

claims.claim: Costco is praised for being efficient, elegant, fun to shop at, and offering great value with products like Kirkland.
claims.quote: And you say that Costco is not just efficient, but elegant. FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE: Oh yeah, it's great. It's fun to be there, fun to shop there. You save money. You get great products, you get great value. You see the same people there. And I think the shopping is sort of an adventure. It's kind of fun. And they put things in the store just to get you back.
claims.speaker: FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE

claims.claim: The speaker notes that McDonald's responded with a form letter to a complaint about a bad experience, contrasting it with Constellation Brands' heroic response.
claims.quote: And then I did the same thing to McDonald's and talked about something terrible that happened there. And I got a form letter back-- sorry for your bad experience and just nothing. But you know, that's sort of a heroic response-- just going overboard, bending over backwards to make people happy.
claims.speaker: FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE

claims.claim: Constellation Brands sent a gift certificate to the speaker after a bad wine experience, leading him to buy more stock and make a huge profit.
claims.quote: And by golly, Constellation Brands sent me a gift certificate for Costco to give me my money back. You know, I just made a huge profit on it and bought more stock.
claims.speaker: FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE

claims.claim: Amazon is listed alongside airlines and Starbucks as a company that operates throughout the world and has a large number of people to cover.
claims.quote: And that's certainly been the case of airlines and of Starbucks, Amazon-- you know, all these companies operate throughout the world. And you know, you used to talk about the law of large numbers. Well, hell, you need to own a stock that has a large number, because there are a large number of people in the world and a large number of square miles to cover, and you've got to get out there before someone beats you to it.
claims.speaker: FREDERICK "SHAD" ROWE

And if people say, well, the market is very overpriced, and the NASDAQ sells at 33 times earnings or whatever it sells at-- well, you know, what's the yield on a 10-year government? 3%
Well, I'd just want to see how you can pay 10 times what you thought it was eventually going to earn.
